report:
Contrary to that initial impression, major clinical evidence demonstrates that the answer is **yes**: heavy current and former smokers **are less likely to die of lung cancer** if they undergo regular screening with low-dose computed tomography (LDCT). 

Key evidence supporting this conclusion includes:

1. **National Lung Screening Trial (NLST):** This landmark randomized trial of over 53,000 high-risk individuals showed a **20% reduction in lung cancer mortality** among participants screened annually with LDCT compared to those receiving standard chest X-rays ([NEJM NLST Study](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1102873)).
2. **NELSON Trial:** A large European randomized trial confirmed these findings, demonstrating a **24% reduction in lung cancer mortality** among high-risk men (and up to 33% in women) who received volume-based LDCT screening compared to no screening ([NEJM NELSON Study](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1911793)).
3. **U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF):** Based on systematic reviews of randomized controlled trials, the USPSTF recommends annual LDCT screening for adults aged 50 to 80 with a 20 pack-year smoking history. They concluded with moderate certainty that regular LDCT screening provides a substantial net benefit by detecting early-stage, treatable cancers ([USPSTF Recommendation](https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/lung-cancer-screening); [JAMA Evidence Synthesis](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2777244)).

In summary, regular LDCT screening catches asymptomatic lung cancers at earlier, more treatable stages, significantly lowering the risk of lung cancer death in heavy past and present smokers.
